HOSPITAL INSOLVENCY UNDER THE IBC : CLINICAL MORATORIUM, PATIENT -
DATA TRUSTS, CBDC MICRO -TRANCHES   
Introduction  
When a normal business collapses, delay burns cash; when a hospital fails, delay harms people. 
India’s Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) bring  order to corporate distress through the 
Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP), but the rules were written with factories in mind 
rather than intensive care units. A legal moratorium can pause lawsuits and calls from creditors.1 
It cannot keep oxygen flowing at night, reassure clinicians that surgeries will start on time, or help 
bidders judge clinical risk without mishandling patient records. This essay sets out a 
hospital‑specific plan that fits within the IBC. It proposes thre e linked steps:  a Clinical Moratorium 
to keep emergency care, intensive care, operating theatres, oxygen, blood banks, dialysis, and 
diagnostics running while the statutory clock continues;2  Patient‑Data Trusts so bidders can 
evaluate performance using consented, limited data; and a Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC)  
based micro‑tranches that pay critical suppliers as soon as a service is verified. The aim is simple: 
protect patients, preserve value, and keep the case on time.  
Why Hospitals Require a Sector‑Specific Insolvency Playbook  
A hospital keeps its value only when care is safe and uninterrupted. Even a short disruption in the 
emergency department, intensive care and operating rooms, oxygen deliveries, blood banking, 
dialysis services, or core diagnostics can cancel surgeries, pus h staff to leave, and lower bids. The 
IBC already requires the business to keep running3 and protects essential supplies during the 
moratoriu m.4 However, it defines “essentials” as utilities such as electricity, water, telecom, and 
IT rather than clinical services.5 This essay translates those general rules into clear, 
hospital‑specific steps that a resolution professional (RP) can apply from day one, so patient safety 
and financial value rest on the same foundation.  
 
1 The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (31 of 2016) s 14(1).  
2 The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (31 of 2016) s 12.  
3 The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (31 of 2016) s 20. 
4 The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (31 of 2016) s 1 4(2). 
5 Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 
2016 reg 32.  Pillar I: Statutory Clinical Moratorium within the Existing CIRP Timeline  
A Clinical Moratorium is a practical rule rather than a loophole or a delay. When CIRP begins, the 
RP names the hospital’s critical services, namely emergency care, intensive care, operating 
theatres, oxygen and vacuum lines, the blood bank, dialysis, and core diagnostics such as imaging 
and laboratory services, and protects these services as strictly as power and water.  The timelines 
do not change because the case still runs within the IBC limits. The moratorium simply defines 
what continuity means in a hospital so that direct patient care is not delayed by legal processes.6 
Payments stay strict and predictable. Pay for current use now and route older dues through the 
resolution plan. Vendors are paid once the delivery is verified. A short grace window, measured 
in hours, prevents paperwork from creating clinical risk, while p reserving the vendor’s right to 
stop new deliveries if current bills are not paid.7 
Accountability focuses on results rather than paperwork. If anyone asks the court for more time, 
that request should be earned by showing that continuity actually improved. Use three simple 
checks. First, were beds and other critical services available whe n patients needed them? Second, 
did cancellations of surgeries and other time‑sensitive procedures go down? Third, did expected 
recovery for creditors improve compared with liquidation value because care continued safely? 
These checks keep the focus on wha t matters: direct patient care and value for stakeholders.8 
Pillar II: Patient‑Data Trusts for Privacy‑Preserving Diligence  
Bidders cannot price a hospital from revenue and cost lines alone. They also need a clear picture 
of the care being delivered , who is treated, what outcomes are achieved, and what  kind of  risk 
exist. Most of this information present  inside electronic medical records and related clinical 
systems. Because these records are sensitive and governed by consent‑based law, a neutral 
governance layer is required.9 
 
6 The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (31 of 2016) ss 12, 20.  
7 The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (31 of 2016) s 14(2A).  
8 Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Ltd v Satish Kumar Gupta  (2020) 8 SCC 531.  
9 Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (22 of 2023) ss 6(1), 6(4), 6(7) – (9). A Patient‑Data Trust provides that layer without creating a new database. The hospital keeps the 
records, and the trust coordinates lawful access. Using existing health‑data consent mechanisms,10 
the trust grants time‑limited and purpose‑limited access to only the fields required for diligence, 
such as case‑mix and payer‑mix profiles, infection rates, length‑of‑stay patterns, equipment 
uptime, and discharge outcomes. Identities are not shared. Eve ry access is logged from start to 
finish, and consent can be withdrawn.11 In practice, bidders see the “what” of clinical performance 
while the “who” remains protected. This reduces privacy risk, increases bidder confidence, and 
supports stronger pricing without compromising rights.  
Pillar III: CBDC Micro‑Tranches for Just‑in‑Time Funding of Clinical Essentials  
Hospitals run on minute‑by‑minute logistics. If an oxygen refill is acknowledged at 6:10 p.m., the 
supplier should not wait days to be paid. Micro‑tranches close this timing gap by putting a small 
programmable escrow inside the resolution plan. If a digita l‑rupee (CBDC) wallet is available, it 
serves as the payment rail;12 if not, a tightly specified bank escrow with API‑based releases serves 
the same role. Each clinically important event  for example an oxygen cylinder signed in on the 
ward, pharmacy stock rising above a safety threshold, or an implant staged in an operating theatre  
which triggers a small, pre‑set payment from escrow. Weekly caps, automated alerts, and 
clawbacks handle disputes and discourage misuse. In short, the rule “pay current dues to keep 
essentials flowing” happens in near real time, within minutes rather than after a committee 
meeting.13 This keeps direct patient care stable and preserves the hospital’s going‑concern value.  
Synthesis and Implementation: Doctrinal Fit within the IBC Framework  
All three elements sit within powers the IBC already gives RPs and courts. A resolution plan must 
show how operations will continue, how stakeholders are protected, and how performance will be

cenbank -says-2024 -04-05/ accessed 1 2 October 2025.  supervised.14 The Clinical Moratorium turns those general duties into concrete clinical obligations 
and assigns responsibility for keeping them in place. The Data‑Trust clause codifies lawful, 
audited, limited‑purpose diligence access without bulk copying or open‑ended  permissions. The 
Digital Escrow clause defines eligible vendors and the verification events that trigger 
micro‑payments, with caps and clawbacks built in. An outcome‑linked extension clause ties any 
extra time to measurable gains in continuity and expecte d recovery, so the statutory clock is 
respected and extensions buy real public value rather than breathing space alone.  
Anticipated Objections and Structured Responses  
Privacy worries are addressed by design. The Patient‑Data Trust does not centrali ze records; it 
uses explicit consent, narrows access to what is strictly necessary for a short window, logs every 
read, and allows revocation. Questions about CBDC readiness are handled by being rail‑agnostic: 
where digital‑rupee wallets are practical, they  are used; where they are not, a programmable bank 
escrow achieves the same operational effect. Fears that these mechanisms might slow the case 
miss the point. The Clinical Moratorium keeps the matter on the statutory clock by removing 
hesitation at the po int of care; micro‑payments prevent standoffs with essential vendors that would 
otherwise force adjournments; and any extension must be justified with hard numbers rather than 
hopeful assurances. Once running, clinicians know supplies will arrive and be pa id for, bidders 
know what they are buying, and courts see objective indicators rather than ambiguity. Finally, 
emergency -care jurisprudence15 and national standards under the Clinical Establishments Act16 
reinforce the principle that critical care must not be interrupted, which aligns with the Clinical 
Moratorium’s focus on safety during CIRP.   
Conclusion  
The IBC promises speed, order, and outcomes better than liquidation. In healthcare, that promise 
is inseparable from patient safety. A Clinical Moratorium stabilizes  the services that define a 
hospital’s value; Patient‑Data Trusts allow bidders to understand performance without exposing 
identities; and CBDC‑style micro‑tranches, or their escrow equivalent, move money at the speed 
 
14 IBC ss 12, 14, 20; IBBI (CIRP) Regulations 2016 reg 32.  
15 Pt Parmanand Katara v Union of India  (1989) 4 SCC 286.  
16 Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 (23 of 2010).  of care. Together, these elements turn the usual tension between speed, value, and protection into 
a self‑reinforcing triangle. Because each piece fits within the tools the law already provides, this 
is a practical path to hospital resolutions that are fas t, valuable, and safe by 2030.
